strengths: The focus on sparse whitened mean differences under strong covariance spikes addresses an identifiable audience in high-dimensional classification and factor models. This setting offers useful insights without requiring state-of-the-art performance.

The core LDA procedure is straightforward: estimate structured whitening, screen transformed coordinates, and apply a linear discriminant. Retaining the bulk eigenspace during whitening allows information outside the leading principal components to contribute.

Using two-to-infinity perturbation bounds to analyze whitening and feature screening is well motivated. Explicit assumptions, algorithm descriptions, and detailed derivations make the main approach understandable.

The experimental design includes several covariance structures, 200 Monte Carlo replications with standard deviations, established baselines, two gene-expression datasets, and a sensitivity analysis for the number of spikes.
weaknesses: Necessary correction: The QDA reduction from Eq. (5.3) to Eq. (5.5) is generally invalid. Sparse whitened means do not imply that covariance discrimination is confined to their support. The omitted quantity ||[W1 Z] outside A0||² − ||[W2 Z] outside A0||² need not vanish or be constant. For example, take Σ_i = p uuᵀ + σ_i² I, u = (1,…,1)/√p, μ_i = σ_i(e1−e2), and distinct fixed σ_i. These satisfy the stated QDA structural and sparsity conditions, with A0 = {1,2}. Full observations distinguish the bulk variances with error tending to zero, whereas the screened population score retains only finitely many Gaussian projections and has nonzero optimal error. Estimating an intercept cannot recover the discarded information. Theorem 6 and the advertised QDA guarantee therefore require a different procedure, additional restrictions, or removal.

Necessary correction: The supplied proof does not establish Theorem 3 as stated. Section 8.4 ends with convergence in probability of discriminant scores under log(n) log(p) = o(n), whereas the theorem asserts almost-sure convergence of conditional classification risk under Assumptions 1–4, which require only log(p) = o(n). The additional condition log(p) = O(n) in the theorem does not resolve this discrepancy. Both the growth condition and the passage to almost-sure conditional-risk convergence need justification or narrower claims. The abstract should also clearly reflect the fixed sparsity actually analyzed; Remark 1 explicitly leaves growing sparsity unproved.

Necessary correction: Section 7.3 overstates Bayes optimality for elliptical distributions with unequal class priors. Even with a common monotone radial density h and sub-Gaussian tails, the likelihood ratio involves log h(r1) − log h(r2), which generally does not reduce to the Gaussian linear rule with a log-prior threshold. Covariance concentration does not establish this decision-theoretic equivalence. Restrict the assertion to suitable conditions, such as equal priors and a common strictly decreasing radial density, or derive the appropriate classifier.

Necessary correction: The numerical evidence contains discrepancies that require an audit. Under the stated Model 2, the squared Mahalanobis mean separation is 10(1+9ρ)/[(1−ρ)(1+19ρ)]. With equal priors, this gives Bayes error approximately 0.0196% at ρ = 0.9, while Table 3 reports an oracle error of 5.40%. The latter is incompatible with the stated model and replication count. Several entries also repeat exactly between ρ = 0.7 and 0.8 in Tables 1–2, and the claim of highest accuracy throughout Model 1 contradicts Table 1. Correct the model specification, implementation, or tables and reassess the empirical conclusions.

Optional improvements: Timing and memory measurements, including preprocessing and tuning, would help assess the claimed computational advantages. Diagnostics of the covariance assumptions on the real datasets would also improve practical guidance. These additions are separate from the substantive mathematical and numerical corrections needed for acceptance.
